Week 5: Handling Big Data Files — YARN, File Formats & Optimization

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. Why this week matters

After HDFS (storage) and MapReduce (processing), two questions decide speed in real life:

  • Scheduling → how do many jobs/teams share one big cluster fairly? (YARN)
  • Format → how do we store data so a query reads only what it needs? (Parquet / ORC / Avro)

2. Hadoop 1.x vs Hadoop 2.x (YARN)

Hadoop 1.x problem: one JobTracker did everything (resource management + job scheduling + monitoring).

  • Only MapReduce could run (no Spark/Tez).
  • Single bottleneck → max about 4,000 nodes.

Fix (Hadoop 2.0, 2013): split resource management from computation → YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator).

Point Hadoop 1 YARN (Hadoop 2)
Max nodes ~4,000 10,000+
Frameworks MapReduce only Any (Spark, Tez, Flink…)
Resource unit Slot (fixed) Container (flexible)
Job manager Inside JobTracker Per-app ApplicationMaster
Resource Manager HA No Yes (ZooKeeper)

📐 Draw: Hadoop 1 vs Hadoop 2

(Left: one big box on top of 3 small boxes. Right: RM on top, 3 NodeManagers below, 2 ApplicationMasters sitting on nodes.)

3. YARN's 3 components (very important)

  1. ResourceManager (RM) — one per cluster, global boss.
    • Scheduler: gives containers to applications (FIFO / Capacity / Fair).
    • ApplicationsManager: accepts job submissions, starts the first container for the AM.
  2. NodeManager (NM) — one per worker node.
    • Launches and watches containers.
    • Sends heartbeats (health + status) to RM.
    • Enforces CPU/RAM limits per container.
  3. ApplicationMaster (AM) — one per job, the job's own manager.
    • Asks RM for containers → tells NMs to run tasks.
    • Watches tasks, re-asks for containers if a task fails, releases them at the end.

Container = a slice of one node = {some vCPUs + some RAM}. Tasks run inside containers. If a task exceeds its memory limit, the NM kills it.

Exam trap: RM = global (1 per cluster). AM = per job.

YARN job flow (6 steps)

  1. Client submits job to RM.
  2. RM launches a container for the AM.
  3. AM registers with RM and requests containers.
  4. AM tells NMs to launch tasks in the containers.
  5. Tasks report status to AM.
  6. AM unregisters when done.

📐 Draw: YARN job execution

Boxes: Client, RM, AM, 3 NMs. Number the arrows 1–6.

YARN fault tolerance

  • NodeManager dies → RM sees missed heartbeats (about 10 min by default) → marks all containers on that node failed → AM asks for new containers elsewhere.
  • AM dies → RM restarts it (default max 2 attempts, yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts). New AM can recover from HDFS checkpoints if the framework supports it (MapReduce yes).
  • RM dies → RM High Availability (YARN 2.4+): Active + Standby RM via ZooKeeper, failover in under ~60 s.
  • Timeline Server: stores history of apps/containers for debugging (RM UI at port 8088).

4. YARN Schedulers

Scheduler How it works Good / bad
FIFO Jobs run in submission order Simple, but one long job starves others
Capacity Cluster split into queues with guaranteed %; can borrow unused capacity Good for many teams (used by Yahoo!, LinkedIn)
Fair All jobs get an equal share; short jobs finish fast Used by Facebook, Twitter
  • Example (a2i): Queue A 60% (nightly batch), Queue B 30% (Spark streaming), Queue C 10% (ad-hoc Hive). B can't steal A's 60%.
  • DRF (Dominant Resource Fairness): fairness when jobs need different resources (CPU-heavy vs RAM-heavy) — looks at each job's dominant resource.

5. Row vs Columnar storage

  • Row store (CSV, JSON): values of one row stored together → a query reading 1 column still reads all columns.
  • Columnar store (Parquet, ORC): values of one column stored together → reads only the needed columns.

📐 Draw: Row vs Column

🧮 Calculation: I/O saved by columnar format

Given in the lecture example: a table has 100 columns and 10 TB of data. The query needs only 3 columns.

  1. Find the fraction of columns needed.3 ÷ 100 = 0.03 = 3%
  2. Estimate Parquet data read. A columnar query can skip the other columns.0.03 × 10 TB = 0.3 TB ≈ 300 GB
  3. Estimate CSV data read. A row-oriented scan reads the complete rows, so use approximately the full 10 TB.
  4. Calculate the I/O speedup.10 TB ÷ 0.3 TB ≈ 33.3× (about 33×)
  5. Calculate I/O reduction.(10 − 0.3) ÷ 10 × 100% = 97%

Conclusion: for a query reading 3 of 100 columns, Parquet can reduce the data read by about 97% compared with a full CSV row scan. Actual performance also depends on compression, filters, storage, and query execution.

6. File formats — comparison table (memorise)

Format Row/Column Schema Splittable Compression Best for
Text / CSV Row External Only with a splittable codec None default Small data, portability
JSON lines Row Self No (raw) External APIs, log ingestion
Avro Row Self-describing (JSON schema) Yes Snappy/Deflate Schema evolution, Kafka → HDFS
Parquet Columnar Self-describing Yes Snappy/Gzip Spark, Presto, ML, analytics
ORC Columnar Self-describing Yes Zlib/Snappy Hive, highest compression, Hive ACID
  • Avro + schema evolution: reader schema vs writer schema. Missing fields use defaults; extra fields are ignored → old consumers don't break when a new field is added (LinkedIn example).
  • Parquet layout: A Parquet file has a header and footer. Between them, data is organised into row groups. Each row group contains a column chunk for each column, and each column chunk is split into pages.
  • Predicate pushdown (query WHERE score > 90):
    1. Read only the footer to get min/max per row group.
    2. Row Group 1 has score in [60, 85] → max 85 < 90 → skip whole group (no I/O).
    3. Row Group 2 has [85, 99] → must read.
    4. Inside it read only the score column chunk.
    • Result: a 10 TB Parquet query may read ~50 GB. Spark does this by default (spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown=true).

7. Compression codecs & splittability

Splittable = HDFS/MapReduce can start reading from the middle of the file without decompressing from the start → many mappers work in parallel.

Codec Speed Ratio Splittable?
Snappy Fast Medium No (but Parquet row groups are)
Gzip Slow High No
LZO Fast Medium Yes (with index)
Bzip2 Slowest Highest Yes
Zstd Fast High No (block-level)

Gzip trap: a 10 GB gzip CSV is processed by exactly 1 mapper → no parallelism. Fix: Parquet + Snappy, or bzip2.

Parallel reading example: row-group based Parquet reads can be split across several workers, while a single gzip-compressed CSV file is generally not splittable for MapReduce.

8. Which format to choose (decision table)

Scenario Format Compression Why
Kafka → HDFS streaming ingest Avro Snappy Schema evolution, append friendly
Spark analytics Parquet Snappy Columnar, pushdown, Spark-native
Hive warehouse ORC Zlib Best compression, ACID, vectorised
Data exchange / APIs Avro or JSON None Readable schema
ML features Parquet Gzip Column-oriented
Archive / cold storage ORC or Parquet Zstd Max compression

bKash example: ingest = Avro → analytics = nightly Parquet+Snappy partitioned by dt=/region= → archive (>2 years) = ORC+Zstd.

9. Research paper: YARN (Vavilapalli et al., 2013, ACM SoCC)

  • 16 authors (Yahoo!, Hortonworks, Microsoft).
  • Contribution 1: 3-layer architecture (RM / NM / AM).
  • Contribution 2: container model, pluggable schedulers, tested at 6,000 nodes, 100,000 tasks, RM handles ~1,000 heartbeats/s, <1 s scheduling latency.
  • Contribution 3: layered fault tolerance + Timeline Server.
  • Legacy: Spark/Tez/Samza on YARN. Kubernetes replaced YARN for new setups but has the same 3-tier idea (global scheduler / node agent / per-app master).

10. Case study: LinkedIn on YARN (2013–2016)

  • Before: 3 separate clusters (Hive MR, Spark, Samza) → under-used, 3× ops cost.
  • After: one 5,000-node YARN cluster with Capacity Scheduler queues.
  • Results: 500 TB/day, up to 400,000 containers, PYMK (People You May Know) recompute 18 h → 4 h.
  • Utilisation 45% → 78%.

LinkedIn YARN case study — check the utilisation change. The notes report utilisation rising from 45% to 78%.

  1. Compare new with old utilisation: 78 ÷ 45 ≈ 1.733.
  2. Remove the original 1.0 baseline: 1.733 − 1 = 0.733.
  3. Convert to a percentage: 0.733 × 100% ≈ 73.3%.

Result: roughly 73% more work could be handled at the reported utilisation ratio on the same hardware. Utilisation ratio is a proxy for capacity, not proof of a 73% improvement for every workload.

Lessons: consolidation ↑ utilisation; Capacity Scheduler gives SLAs; pre-emption needs tuning (30 s grace); "YARN is the OS, frameworks are processes".

11. 🧮 YARN capacity planning (live exercise, solved step by step)

Worked practice example — using the assumptions stated here. This calculation demonstrates how RAM and CPU both limit the number of YARN containers; it is an expanded worked exercise, not a verbatim quote from a slide.

Given: 5,000 nodes; each node has 64 GB RAM and 16 vCPU. Queue shares: production 40%, Spark 25%, Samza 15%, ad-hoc 10%, reserve 10%. Container sizes: Hive mapper = 4 GB + 2 vCPU; Spark executor = 8 GB + 4 vCPU; Samza task = 2 GB + 1 vCPU.

Method for each queue

  1. Allocated nodes = 5,000 × queue share.
  2. Total RAM = allocated nodes × 64 GB; total CPU = allocated nodes × 16 vCPU.
  3. RAM capacity = total RAM ÷ RAM required by one container.
  4. CPU capacity = total CPU ÷ vCPU required by one container.
  5. Maximum containers = the smaller of RAM capacity and CPU capacity. The limiting resource is the bottleneck.
Queue/workloadNodesTotal RAMTotal CPULimit by RAMLimit by CPUMax containers
Production · Hive mapper (40%)5,000 × 0.40 = 2,0002,000 × 64 = 128,000 GB2,000 × 16 = 32,000 vCPU128,000 ÷ 4 = 32,00032,000 ÷ 2 = 16,00016,000 (CPU bottleneck)
Spark executor (25%)5,000 × 0.25 = 1,2501,250 × 64 = 80,000 GB1,250 × 16 = 20,000 vCPU80,000 ÷ 8 = 10,00020,000 ÷ 4 = 5,0005,000 (CPU bottleneck)
Samza task (15%)5,000 × 0.15 = 750750 × 64 = 48,000 GB750 × 16 = 12,000 vCPU48,000 ÷ 2 = 24,00012,000 ÷ 1 = 12,00012,000 (CPU bottleneck)

Check: can the production queue run 10,000 Hive mappers?

  1. Per node, RAM allows 64 ÷ 4 = 16 Hive mappers.
  2. Per node, CPU allows 16 ÷ 2 = 8 Hive mappers.
  3. CPU is the bottleneck, so use 8 mappers per node.
  4. Nodes needed = 10,000 ÷ 8 = 1,250 nodes, within the production allocation of 2,000 nodes.

No container type was specified for the ad-hoc queue, so its container capacity is not calculated here. The 10% reserve remains unallocated.

12. 🧮 Exam-style: telecom CDR migration (A1)

Problem from the Week 5 analytical question: the company stores 10 TB/day as gzip-compressed CSV. A query selects 4 of 80 columns and currently takes 6 hours.

Part A — explain the bottlenecks

  1. CSV is row-oriented, so selecting four columns can still require reading the full rows.
  2. Gzip-compressed CSV is not splittable in the normal Hadoop MapReduce input path. A large gzip file therefore cannot be divided into independent input splits in the same way as a splittable format, limiting parallelism.

Part B — estimate the column-based I/O

  1. Needed column fraction = 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05 = 5%.
  2. Estimated Parquet data read = 5% × 10 TB = 0.5 TB ≈ 500 GB.
  3. Estimated I/O reduction = (10 − 0.5) ÷ 10 × 100% = 95%.
  4. Approximate I/O ratio = 10 TB ÷ 0.5 TB = 20× less data read.

Recommended migration: convert to Parquet + Snappy, partition by date (for example, dt=YYYY-MM-DD), and use the Capacity Scheduler for a shared multi-team cluster. The 20× figure is an estimate of column-scan I/O, not a guarantee that the full query will run 20× faster; partition pruning, compression, CPU, shuffle, and query plan also matter.

13. 🧮 YARN failure trace (A2: NM2 with 5 containers dies)

  1. NM2 stops sending heartbeats to RM.
  2. After the timeout (~10 min) RM marks NM2 as lost.
  3. RM marks the 5 containers on NM2 as failed.
  4. RM tells the AM(s) that those containers are lost.
  5. AM re-requests 5 new containers from RM.
  6. RM Scheduler allocates them on healthy nodes.
  7. AM tells those NMs to re-run the 5 tasks. (If the AM itself was on NM2, RM restarts the AM first.)

✅ Week 5 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • RM (global) vs NM (per node) vs AM (per job) — most asked.
  • Why YARN: JobTracker was a single bottleneck, MapReduce only, ~4,000 nodes.
  • Columnar = reads only needed columns; know the 33× / 97% example.
  • Gzip is NOT splittable. Parquet/ORC/Avro are.
  • Avro → schema evolution + Kafka ingest. Parquet → Spark/analytics. ORC → Hive.
  • Predicate pushdown = skip row groups using min/max stats in footer.
  • Be able to draw: YARN flow (6 arrows), Hadoop1 vs 2, row vs column, Parquet layout.
  • Schedulers: FIFO / Capacity (queues, guaranteed %) / Fair (equal share).
  • True/False seen: Parquet is row-oriented → False; Gzip splittable → False; ORC best for Hive → True.

Week 6: Apache Spark — RDDs, DataFrames & In-Memory Computing

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. Why Spark? MapReduce is slow for repeated passes

  • MapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS before the next step.
  • Machine learning and graph algorithms are iterative (read the same data again and again) → huge disk I/O.
  • Spark idea: load data into RAM once (cache) and iterate in memory.

🧮 K-Means, 50 GB data, 100 iterations

Given in the Week 6 exercise: 50 GB of training data; 100 K-Means iterations.

MapReduce — step by step

  1. Each iteration reads the 50 GB dataset and writes a 50 GB result.I/O per iteration = 50 GB + 50 GB = 100 GB
  2. Repeat this I/O for 100 iterations.100 × 100 GB = 10,000 GB ≈ 10 TB

Spark — step by step

  1. Iteration 1 reads the 50 GB from HDFS and caches the data in RAM.
  2. Iterations 2–100 reuse the cached dataset, assuming it fits in memory and remains cached.
  3. HDFS read I/O is therefore approximately 50 GB (initial read only)

Disk-I/O comparison: 10,000 GB ÷ 50 GB = 200× less HDFS I/O for Spark under these assumptions. This is an I/O comparison, not a promise of 200× shorter wall-clock time.

🧮 Time estimate (A1 from the slides: HDFS 500 MB/s, RAM 5,000 MB/s)

Given in the Week 6 exercise: HDFS throughput = 500 MB/s; RAM cache-read throughput = 5,000 MB/s; data = 50 GB; iterations = 100. Use decimal units, so 1 GB = 1,000 MB.

1. MapReduce time estimate

  1. From the previous calculation, total read + write I/O = 10 TB = 10,000,000 MB.
  2. Time = data I/O ÷ throughput.10,000,000 MB ÷ 500 MB/s = 20,000 s
  3. Convert seconds to hours.20,000 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 5.56 hours (about 5.6 h)

2. Spark time estimate (if 50 GB fits in RAM)

  1. Initial HDFS read: 50,000 MB ÷ 500 MB/s = 100 s.
  2. Each later iteration reads from RAM: 50,000 MB ÷ 5,000 MB/s = 10 s.
  3. There are 99 later iterations: 99 × 10 s = 990 s.
  4. Total estimated I/O time = 100 + 990 = 1,090 s ≈ 18.2 minutes.

3. Estimated I/O-time speedup

20,000 s ÷ 1,090 s ≈ 18.3× (about 18×)

Limit of the estimate: it considers I/O time only; it excludes CPU work, task scheduling, serialization, shuffle, cache eviction, and other overhead. Spark may not win on a single-pass job or when the dataset does not fit in memory.

📐 Draw: MapReduce vs Spark

2. Spark history (short)

  • 2009 Matei Zaharia (UC Berkeley AMPLab) sees MapReduce is bad for iterative ML.
  • 2010 HotCloud paper "Spark: Cluster Computing with Working Sets".
  • 2012 RDD paper (NSDI) — Best Paper.
  • 2013 donated to Apache; Databricks founded.
  • 2014 100 TB sort record (23 min vs 72 min Hadoop).

3. Spark architecture — 3 parts

  1. Driver Program — runs main(), creates SparkContext/SparkSession, builds the DAG, schedules tasks.
  2. Cluster Manager — allocates resources (YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos, Standalone).
  3. Executors — JVM processes on worker nodes; run tasks and store cached partitions.
  • Spark 1.x entry point = SparkContext. Spark 2.x+ = SparkSession (unifies SQL, DataFrames, RDDs).
  • Spark can run on YARN but not only on YARN (T/F: False).

📐 Draw

4. RDD — Resilient Distributed Dataset

Definition: a read-only, partitioned collection of records created only by (1) loading from stable storage (HDFS/S3) or (2) transforming another RDD.

5 properties (learn as ILPLR):

  • Immutable — never changed in place (T/F: "RDDs are mutable" = False).
  • Partitioned — split across executors for parallel work.
  • Lazy — transformations run only when an action is called.
  • Lineage — remembers how it was built from parent RDDs.
  • Resilient — lost partitions are recomputed from lineage, not replicated.

Fault tolerance: HDFS = keep 3 copies. RDD = re-derive the lost data from the recipe (lineage). "The computation is the backup."

Recovery steps (lost Partition 2):

  1. Spark detects the lost partition.
  2. Looks up lineage: mappedRDD ← filteredRDD ← inputRDD.
  3. Re-reads that partition of the input from HDFS.
  4. Re-applies filter, then map.
  5. Partition restored — whole job is not restarted.

Trade-off: cheap for narrow dependencies; expensive for wide ones (many parents). Long lineage → checkpoint to HDFS.

📐 Draw: lineage

5. Transformations vs Actions + Lazy evaluation

Transformation Action
Runs when? Lazy (only records the plan) Eager (triggers the job)
Returns A new RDD A value to driver / writes output
Examples map, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, cache collect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach

Rule: nothing executes until an action is called.

Lazy evaluation benefits (when action runs, Spark):

  1. Looks at the whole DAG and optimises.
  2. Pipelines narrow steps (filter+map in one pass, no intermediate disk write).
  3. Runs only the partitions needed.

Example: rdd.filter(x > 1000).first() → Spark stops after finding the first match; without laziness it would filter the whole dataset first.

(Common wrong belief: "map() runs immediately" → MCQ answer is lazily evaluated.)

6. Narrow vs Wide dependencies

Narrow Wide
Each output partition depends on ≤ 1 input partition Many input partitions
Shuffle (network) No Yes
Stage Same stage (pipelined) New stage boundary
Examples map, filter, flatMap, union, coalesce groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, repartition, distinct
Recovery Recompute 1 parent partition Recompute all parents (expensive)

Tip: prefer reduceByKey over groupByKey — reduceByKey combines locally before shuffle (like a MapReduce Combiner) → less network traffic.

📐 Draw

7. Persistence (cache) & partitioning (from RDD paper)

  • Cache an RDD only if used in more than one action (else wastes RAM, causes eviction — LRU).
  • Storage levels: MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, DISK_ONLY, MEMORY_ONLY_SER, OFF_HEAP.
  • Partitioners: Hash (default: key.hashCode % numPartitions), Range (used by sortByKey), Custom (co-partition two RDDs to avoid shuffle in join).

8. PySpark examples (know the pattern)

Word count:

lines  = sc.textFile("hdfs:///data/corpus/*.txt")     # load
words  = lines.flatMap(lambda l: l.split())           # transformation
pairs  = words.map(lambda w: (w, 1))                  # transformation
counts = pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)        # transformation (wide)
counts.saveAsTextFile("hdfs:///output/wordcount/")    # ACTION -> runs now

Why each step: flatMap splits lines into words; map makes (word,1); reduceByKey adds the 1s per word; the action triggers everything.

9. DataFrames & Spark SQL

  • DataFrame = distributed table with named columns + schema (built on RDDs).
  • Uses Catalyst optimizer (predicate pushdown, join reordering, constant folding) and Tungsten (efficient code generation).
  • 10–100× faster than RDDs for structured data. Use DataFrames/SQL unless you need low-level control.
  • Reads Parquet, ORC, CSV, JSON, Hive tables, JDBC.

10. Spark ecosystem (📐 draw as layers)

  • MLlib — distributed ML (k-means, logistic regression, random forest).
  • Structured Streaming — stream as an ever-growing table; same API as batch; event-time windows, watermarks, exactly-once with Kafka.
  • GraphX — PageRank, connected components.
  • HBase is NOT part of Spark (MCQ).

11. MapReduce vs Spark (full table)

Point MapReduce Spark
Intermediate data Disk (HDFS) Memory (spills to disk if needed)
Model Map + Reduce only map, filter, join, SQL, ML, streaming
Languages Java mainly Python, Scala, Java, R
Iterative jobs Slow Fast (10–100×)
Fault tolerance Re-run task from HDFS Recompute from lineage
Streaming Not native Structured Streaming
Interactive Not feasible (>30 s) Sub-second
Learning curve Low (2 functions) Moderate

Use MapReduce for stable single-pass huge batch jobs. Use Spark for ML, graphs, interactive, streaming, or >2 iterations on same data.

12. Research papers & case study (Part 2)

Paper 1 – Zaharia 2010 (HotCloud): key idea = working set reused across parallel operations → keep in RAM. Paper 2 – Zaharia 2012 (NSDI, Best Paper): formal definition of RDD + lineage fault tolerance.

Benchmarks (RDD paper):

  • Logistic regression, 10 iterations: Hadoop 127 s/iter vs Spark 0.96 s/iter → 127 ÷ 0.96 = ≈ 132×.
  • K-means: Hadoop 150 s vs Spark 5 s → 150 ÷ 5 = 30×.

Case study: Databricks Daytona GraySort (Nov 2013) — sort 100 TB.

Hadoop (Yahoo! 2012) Spark (Databricks)
Time 72 min 23 min
Nodes 2,100 206

Databricks Daytona GraySort comparison — the table reports 100 TB sorted in 72 minutes using 2,100 nodes (Hadoop) and in 23 minutes using 206 nodes (Spark).

  1. Time ratio: 72 ÷ 23 ≈ 3.13×. Spark completed the benchmark in about one-third of the time.
  2. Node-count ratio: 2,100 ÷ 206 ≈ 10.19×. Spark used about one-tenth as many nodes.
  3. Approximate per-node efficiency ratio: (2,100 × 72) ÷ (206 × 23) ≈ 31.9×, or about 32× under this benchmark comparison.
  4. Throughput for the 100 TB Spark run: 100 TB ÷ 23 min ≈ 4.35 TB/min.
  5. RAM installed on the Spark cluster: 206 nodes × 244 GB/node = 50,264 GB ≈ 50.3 TB.

These are historical benchmark figures under the paper's test conditions; they should not be generalised to all Spark and Hadoop jobs.

Why Spark won: sort-based shuffle (less disk I/O), used all 8 SSDs for shuffle, off-heap sort buffers (avoid GC), single wide transformation (fewer stages).

Lessons: in-memory is a multiplier (10–100× iterative, only 2–5× for single-pass over data bigger than RAM); shuffle is the bottleneck — minimise wide dependencies.

13. 🧮 Exam-style: RDD failure (A2)

Pipeline: input → filteredRDD → mappedRDD → reducedRDD, 10 partitions. Executor holding partitions 3 and 7 of reducedRDD crashes.

  1. Driver detects the lost executor (heartbeat/task failure).
  2. Marks partitions 3 and 7 of reducedRDD as lost.
  3. Uses lineage to find parents.
  4. If narrow dependency: recompute only partition 3 and 7 from the matching parent partitions (3 and 7 of the previous RDDs).
  5. If wide (groupByKey): each lost partition needs data from all 10 parent partitions → recompute across all parents. Worst case = recompute everything upstream (up to the input read).
  6. Fix: checkpoint or cache before the shuffle.

✅ Week 6 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • Define RDD + 5 properties; explain "resilient = lineage, not replication".
  • Transformations lazy, actions eager — give 2 examples each.
  • Narrow vs wide → shuffle → stage boundary. Prefer reduceByKey.
  • Know the 200× I/O and ~18× time K-means calculation steps.
  • Driver / Cluster Manager / Executors diagram.
  • Spark not limited to YARN; HBase is not Spark; RDDs immutable.
  • DataFrame = schema + Catalyst → faster than RDD.
  • GraySort numbers: 100 TB, 23 vs 72 min, 206 vs 2,100 nodes.
  • rdd.filter().first() is the standard lazy-evaluation example.

Week 7: Querying Big Data — Hive, HiveQL & SQL-on-Hadoop

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. Why SQL-on-Hadoop?

  • Before Hive (pre-2008): every query = Java MapReduce program (100+ lines even for a simple GROUP BY). Analysts know SQL, not Java. Time-to-insight = days.
  • Hive (Facebook, 2008): write HiveQL (SQL-like) → Hive compiles it into MapReduce / Tez / Spark jobs. "Analyst writes SELECT, Hive writes the distributed job."
  • Facebook numbers (2009–10): 2 PB data, +15 TB/day, 7,500+ queries/day, 200+ analysts.

2. SQL-on-Hadoop tools

Tool Origin Engine Latency Best for
Hive Facebook 2008 MR / Tez / Spark Minutes Batch analytics, big ETL
Presto (Trino) Facebook 2013 In-memory pipeline Seconds Interactive BI dashboards
Impala Cloudera 2012 Native C++ MPP Seconds Low-latency SQL on HDFS/S3
Spark SQL 2014 Catalyst + in-memory Seconds Batch + streaming SQL
Drill MapR 2012 Schema-free Seconds SQL on JSON/Parquet

All share storage: HDFS / S3 / ADLS / GCS.

3. Hive architecture

Components (learn the roles):

  • HiveServer2 — JDBC/ODBC server; logs users in; accepts queries from Beeline, Tableau, Power BI.
  • Driver — runs the pipeline: Parser → Semantic Analyser → Logical Planner → Optimizer → Physical plan.
  • Metastore — a relational DB (MySQL/PostgreSQL) holding all metadata.
  • Execution Engine — MapReduce (legacy default), Tez (DAG, faster) or Spark (SET hive.execution.engine=spark).
  • HDFS — real data. Table = directory; partition = sub-directory.

📐 Draw: Hive architecture

Boxes top to bottom; Metastore on the right with a two-way arrow to the Driver.

How a query is compiled (steps)

  1. Parse HiveQL → Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
  2. Semantic analysis — check column names/types using the Metastore.
  3. Logical plan — Filter → Join → GroupBy → OrderBy.
  4. Optimise — e.g., partition pruning, map-side aggregation.
  5. Physical plan — MapReduce/Tez/Spark job(s).
  6. Submit to YARN, read HDFS, write result. (So: Hive does not run SQL directly on HDFS — T/F: False.)

4. The Metastore (control plane)

Stores: database/table definitions, partition info + HDFS paths, SerDe (how to parse file format), table statistics (row count, min/max, nulls — used by optimizer), privileges, bucket count.

  • Without Metastore Hive cannot answer any query → run it highly available.
  • Schema info is in the Metastore not the NameNode (NameNode only has HDFS block metadata).
  • Spotify: >1 million tables, 600 billion events/day. If Metastore corrupts, data on HDFS is fine but nobody can query it.
  • Today the Metastore is the universal catalogue for Spark, Presto, Trino, Athena.
  • SerDe = Serializer/Deserializer: bytes ↔ rows (e.g., LazySimpleSerDe, JsonSerDe, AvroSerDe, ParquetHiveSerDe, OrcSerDe, RegexSerDe).

5. Schema-on-Read vs Schema-on-Write

Point Schema-on-Write (MySQL) Schema-on-Read (Hive)
Schema checked At INSERT/LOAD At SELECT (query time)
Bad data Rejected Stored; query returns NULL
Flexibility Rigid Flexible, many schemas on same files
Write speed Slower Fast (just copy file)
Query speed Faster Slower (parse each time)
Use OLTP (orders, banking) OLAP (logs, reports)
  • Advantage: load raw logs now, decide schema later; no ETL at ingest.
  • Risk: errors are silent — text "abc" in an amount column gives NULL, not an error. Add downstream checks (Great Expectations, dbt tests).

6. HiveQL vs SQL

Feature SQL (RDBMS) HiveQL
Schema On write On read
ACID Full Limited — ORC transactional tables only
UPDATE/DELETE Any row Only ACID tables
Indexing B-tree, hash Partitions + Buckets
Sub-queries Correlated OK Non-correlated mostly
Latency Milliseconds Minutes (MR) / seconds (Tez/Spark)
Scale TBs PBs
Workload OLTP OLAP

Misconception: HiveQL ≠ millisecond SQL. COUNT(*) on 1 TB may take 5–10 min on MapReduce. Use Presto/Spark SQL for interactive.

7. HiveQL code you may need

External table (dropping table keeps the data in HDFS):

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE transactions (
  txn_id BIGINT, user_id STRING, amount DOUBLE, country STRING, txn_date DATE)
ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','
STORED AS ORC
LOCATION '/data/bkash/txns/';

Aggregation (top 5 countries):

SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS total_BDT
FROM transactions
WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2024
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY total_BDT DESC
LIMIT 5;

8. Partitioning

Definition: split table data into separate HDFS sub-directories by column value. A query filtering on the partition column reads only matching directories (partition pruning).

  • Choose low-cardinality columns used in WHERE (date, country, region, status).
  • Never partition on high-cardinality columns (user_id, txn_id): 100 M users → 100 M directories → NameNode overflow ("partition explosion").
  • Benefit: avoids full-table scan; cuts job time.

📐 Draw: partition tree

CREATE TABLE sales (txn_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, country STRING)
PARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT) STORED AS ORC;

Dynamic partition insert (rule: partition columns must be LAST in the SELECT):

SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition = true;
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;
INSERT INTO sales PARTITION (year, month)
SELECT txn_id, amount, country, YEAR(sale_date), MONTH(sale_date) FROM raw_sales;

Hive partition-pruning example. Partition keys: dt has 365 possible values and country has 200 possible values. Query: one date and three countries (BD, IN, US).

  1. Maximum possible date-country combinations: 365 × 200 = 73,000 possible partitions.
  2. The query filters to one date and three countries, so it needs at most 1 × 3 = 3 matching partitions.
  3. Fraction read: 3 ÷ 73,000 ≈ 0.0000411.
  4. Convert to a percentage: 0.0000411 × 100% ≈ 0.0041%.

73,000 is the maximum number of possible combinations; real tables may have fewer populated partitions. Actual data read also depends on partition pruning and file layout.

9. Bucketing

Definition: split each partition into a fixed number of files using a hash of a column.

  1. CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO N BUCKETS.
  2. Row goes to bucket k = hash(column) % N.
  3. Same bucket number in two tables holds rows that will join.
  • Main benefit: Bucket Map Join — join bucket i of A with bucket i of B only; no full shuffle. Both tables need the same bucket count on the join key.
  • Bucketing does not skip directories (that is partitioning).
Partitioning Bucketing
Splits by Column value → directories Hash → files
Helps Skip data (filter queries) Joins, sampling
Column type Low cardinality High cardinality OK
Risk Too many dirs Bad bucket count

Use both together: e.g., e-commerce table partitioned by txn_date, bucketed by user_id.

CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS STORED AS ORC;

10. Presto (Meta, 2013) — why faster than Hive+MR

  1. No intermediate disk writes — data flows in memory as a pipeline.
  2. Vectorised execution (batches of ~1,024 rows).
  3. Cost-based optimizer (uses stats).
  4. Connectors — one query across HDFS, Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3.
  • Latency: Hive+MR 5–15 min vs Presto 5–60 s.

📐 Draw

11. Research papers (Thusoo et al.)

2009 VLDB — Hive design goals: (1) familiarity (close to SQL), (2) extensibility (SerDes, UDFs), (3) performance (partition pruning, bucketing), (4) fault tolerance (relies on MR/HDFS). 2010 ICDE — petabyte production: map-side aggregation, skew join handling, indexes, ANALYZE TABLE stats, 7,500+ queries/day.

Map-side aggregation example. Query: SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY country, with 50 million rows and 200 countries.

  1. Without partial aggregation: about 50,000,000 row-level records may be sent through the shuffle.
  2. With aggregation in each mapper: each mapper can combine rows into partial (country, count) pairs, with at most 200 country keys per mapper.
  3. Simplified raw-row-to-group comparison: 50,000,000 ÷ 200 = 250,000.

Interpret carefully: 250,000× is the raw-row-to-final-group ratio, not a guaranteed network-shuffle speedup. Actual shuffled pairs depend on how many mappers run and the degree of local aggregation.

Later: ORC format (2013), LLAP (2016, sub-second Hive-on-Tez), Hive-on-Spark (2015).

12. Case study: Spotify Discover Weekly (2015–2018)

  • ~3 billion events/day via Kafka → HDFS; 30 M songs; 2 billion playlists.
  • Luigi = Spotify's Python workflow scheduler (tasks declare output path + dependencies; skips tasks whose output exists).
  • Three signals: (1) playlist co-occurrence (HiveQL: songs appearing together in > N playlists), (2) NLP/Word2Vec on artist text, (3) audio embeddings + cosine similarity (Annoy).
  • Lessons: HiveQL for feature engineering, Spark for iterative ML (ALS); partitioning play_events by week cut co-occurrence query 8 h → 2 h; cold start for new songs is still hard.

ALS model-size estimate from the Spotify case discussion. Users = 75 million; songs = 30 million; rank k = 50; each factor value uses 4 bytes.

  1. User factor matrix: 75,000,000 × 50 = 3,750,000,000 floats. Memory: 3.75 billion × 4 bytes = 15 billion bytes ≈ 15 GB (decimal units).
  2. Song factor matrix: 30,000,000 × 50 = 1,500,000,000 floats. Memory: 1.5 billion × 4 bytes = 6 billion bytes ≈ 6 GB.
  3. Total factor memory: 15 GB + 6 GB = 21 GB, before metadata, replication, temporary data, and framework overhead.
  4. Cluster RAM stated in the example: 5,000 nodes × 64 GB = 320,000 GB ≈ 320 TB.

ALS stores two low-rank factor matrices rather than the full users-by-songs matrix, which is why the model representation is much smaller.

13. 🧮 Exam-style design (A1: 5 TB e-commerce table)

Columns: txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date. Needs: daily revenue by country/date, and join with 10 M-row user table on user_id.

  1. Partition by txn_date (and country if few countries) — daily reports filter on these, low cardinality.
  2. Bucket by user_id — join key, high cardinality (never partition on it).
  3. Step 1 — estimate one daily partition:
    5 TB = 5,000 GB
    5,000 GB ÷ 365 days ≈ 13.7 GB per daily partition
  4. Step 2 — estimate each bucket file:
    13.7 GB ÷ 32 buckets ≈ 0.43 GB ≈ 430 MB per bucket
    Choose 32 buckets (a practical power-of-two example) and use the same bucket count/key for the joined user table if a bucket map join is supported by the actual execution plan.
  5. Bucket the user table on user_id into 32 buckets too (same count → bucket map join).
CREATE TABLE txns (txn_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT, product_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, country STRING)
PARTITIONED BY (txn_date DATE)
CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

14. 🧮 Top 5 products by revenue 2023 → MapReduce trace (A2)

SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM txns WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2023
GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5;
  • Job 1 (GROUP BY): Map reads rows (partition-pruned to 2023), filters, emits (product_id, amount); shuffle key = product_id; Reduce sums amounts per product.
  • Job 2 (ORDER BY + LIMIT): Map emits (revenue, product_id); one reducer sorts descending and keeps top 5.
  • Tez instead of MR: same logic as one DAG — no HDFS write between the two jobs, fewer stages, faster.

✅ Week 7 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • Metastore = schema/partition/SerDe/stats in MySQL/PostgreSQL — not NameNode.
  • Hive = batch, not millisecond; compiles to MR/Tez/Spark.
  • Schema-on-read: check at query time; bad data → NULL silently.
  • Partition = directories (prune data); Bucket = hash files (fast joins). Never partition on high-cardinality.
  • Dynamic partition: partition columns last in SELECT.
  • Presto faster because no disk writes between stages, in-memory pipeline.
  • ACID only on ORC transactional tables.
  • Be able to draw Hive architecture and the partition directory tree.
  • Descriptive Q: partition+bucket together in Bangladesh e-commerce (partition by date/district, bucket by user_id).

Week 8: Data Integration at Scale — Kafka, Pipelines & Lambda/Kappa

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. From point-to-point ETL to pipelines

  • Old way: direct ETL connections tightly couple every system. Worked count:
    1. For each of N systems, there are N − 1 other destinations (no self-connection).
    2. With 50 systems: N × (N − 1) = 50 × 49 = 2,450 directed source-to-destination jobs.
    3. This assumes a separate job for each ordered pair; if each unordered pair were counted only once, the count would be different.
    This mesh is brittle, hard to replay, and often relies on nightly batch; Kafka provides a shared event hub so producers and consumers are decoupled.
  • New way: a central message bus (Kafka). Sources publish, consumers subscribe. New consumer = zero change to sources → decoupled and replayable.

📐 Draw

2. Integration tool landscape

Tool Direction Type Use
Sqoop RDBMS ↔ HDFS Batch Nightly bulk DB sync
Flume Logs → HDFS Batch/micro-batch Web server log collection
Kafka Any → Any Real-time stream Event bus, fraud, clickstream, IoT
NiFi Any → Any Visual pipeline No-code routing, IoT edge
Spark Streaming Kafka → HDFS/DB Stream processing Stateful aggregation, joins

3. Sqoop (SQL-to-Hadoop)

  • Bulk transfer between RDBMS (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL) and HDFS/Hive/HBase.
  • Import RDBMS → HDFS (CSV/Avro/Parquet); Export HDFS → RDBMS.
  • Internally runs a MapReduce job; each mapper reads a range of primary-key rows in parallel.
  • Incremental import: only new rows using a check column + last value (e.g., txn_date).
  • bKash: nightly 01:00, 10 M wallet transactions from Oracle → HDFS Parquet partitioned by txn_date.
  • Not real-time (T/F: "Sqoop for real-time streaming" = False).

📐 Draw

4. Flume

Agent = Source → Channel → Sink.

  • Source: reads incoming data (Avro, Syslog, Exec/tail, HTTP).
  • Channel: buffer. Memory (fast, lost if crash) or File (persistent, survives restart).
  • Sink: writes out (HDFS, Kafka, HBase).
  • Topologies: fan-in (many sources → one agent), fan-out (one source → many sinks).
  • Flume = log collection to HDFS. Kafka has stronger durability and replay → Flume often replaced by Kafka.

📐 Draw

5. Apache Kafka — the append-only log

  • Born at LinkedIn (2011): Kreps, Narkhede, Rao. Open-sourced to Apache 2012.
  • Core idea: a distributed, partitioned, replicated append-only commit log.
  • Traditional queue: message deleted after consumption. Kafka: messages kept for a set time (e.g., 7 days) → consumers can replay from offset 0.

Key terms (memorise):

  • Topic — named append-only log for a category of events.
  • Partition — a topic split into P ordered logs → parallelism. Same key → same partition (keeps key order).
  • Offset — integer position of a message in a partition; each consumer tracks its own.
  • Broker — Kafka server storing partitions. Each partition has 1 leader + (R−1) followers; default replication factor R = 3.
  • Producer — writes to a topic (partition by key hash or round-robin).
  • Consumer group — consumers sharing a topic's partitions; each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group.
  • ZooKeeper / KRaft — metadata + leader election (ZooKeeper before Kafka 3.0; KRaft after).
  • 🧮 Max useful consumers in a group = number of partitions P (extra consumers sit idle).

📐 Draw: Kafka topic

Why Kafka is fast (5 reasons)

  1. Sequential disk writes (append-only): about 600 MB/s sequential vs about 100 MB/s random → roughly 6× advantage (Part 2 slide).
  2. Zero-copy (sendfile()): disk → kernel buffer → NIC. 2 copies instead of 4, near-zero CPU.
  3. Batching of messages (batch.size, linger.ms) + batch compression (5–10× for logs).
  4. Partition parallelism — throughput scales with partitions.
  5. Consumer pull + ACK per batch, no per-consumer queues.

Storage detail

Partition = segment files: .log (data) + .index (offset → byte position). Last segment = active; old segments are immutable and deleted after retention (default 7 days).

🧮 Paper benchmark (100-byte messages, one broker) — work out the ratios

Benchmark values reported in the Week 8 Part 2 paper slides (one broker, 100-byte messages; producer and consumer throughput are separate measurements):

SystemProducer MB/sConsumer MB/s
ActiveMQ4.34.0
RabbitMQ14.78.2
Kafka50.522.0

Step 1 — producer throughput ratio

  1. Kafka vs ActiveMQ: 50.5 ÷ 4.3 ≈ 11.7×.
  2. Kafka vs RabbitMQ: 50.5 ÷ 14.7 ≈ 3.4×.

Step 2 — consumer throughput ratio

  1. Kafka vs ActiveMQ: 22.0 ÷ 4.0 = 5.5×.
  2. Kafka vs RabbitMQ: 22.0 ÷ 8.2 ≈ 2.7×.

Step 3 — check producer messages per second

  1. Convert 50.5 MB/s to bytes/s, using decimal MB: 50.5 × 1,000,000 = 50,500,000 bytes/s.
  2. Divide by 100 bytes per message: 50,500,000 ÷ 100 = 505,000 messages/s.

These are historical benchmark figures under the paper's test conditions, not universal modern performance guarantees.

Later Kafka ecosystem tools: Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, Kafka Connect, Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf), idempotent producers/transactions for exactly-once processing, and tiered storage.

Bangladesh examples: bKash can route wallet-credit/wallet-debit topics to fraud detection, balance updates, and HDFS auditing. Pathao can publish GPS pings every 3 seconds to a driver-location topic, partitioned by driver_id.

6. Lambda Architecture (Nathan Marz, 2011)

Goal: accurate historical views and fast real-time views from the same data.

  1. Batch layer — stores the immutable master dataset (HDFS), recomputes batch views (Spark/Hive). Accurate, high latency (hours).
  2. Speed layer — processes new data since last batch (Kafka + Spark Streaming/Flink). Approximate, low latency (seconds).
  3. Serving layer — merges batch + real-time views to answer queries.
  • Query result = batch view (up to N hours ago) UNION real-time view (last N hours).

📐 Draw: Lambda

Strengths: accuracy (recompute from raw), low latency, fault tolerance, separation of concerns. Big weakness: dual code paths — same business logic written twice (batch + speed) and kept in sync (30–40% of effort); two infrastructures; serving layer must merge.

7. Kappa Architecture (Jay Kreps, 2014)

Idea: drop the batch layer if the stream engine can replay history as fast as live data.

  1. Log storage (Kafka with long retention, or Iceberg on S3).
  2. One stream processing engine (Flink/Spark Structured Streaming) = single code path.
  • Reprocess: deploy new job version → start at offset 0 → it catches up to live → swap into production → retire old version.

📐 Draw: Kappa

Lambda vs Kappa

Property Lambda Kappa
Code paths Two (batch + stream) One (stream)
Reprocessing Re-run batch on HDFS Replay Kafka log from offset 0
Complexity High Lower
Batch throughput Very high Limited by stream engine
Use when Complex logic, batch ML, regulatory batch reports Stream engine is fast enough, one code path wanted
Kappa not suitable when — Reprocessing TBs is too slow; batch SQL preferred; regulation needs separate batch reconciliation

8. Data lake & data swamp

Data lake = central store of raw data, any format, no upfront schema (schema-on-read). 4 layers:

  1. Ingestion (Sqoop, Flume, Kafka, NiFi)
  2. Storage (HDFS/S3, zones: raw → processed → curated)
  3. Processing (Spark, Hive, Presto)
  4. Catalogue/Governance (Atlas, Glue, Hive Metastore)
Data lake Data warehouse
Schema On read (no upfront) On write (strict)
Format Raw, any Structured, processed
Use Exploration, ML, raw archive BI / reporting

Data swamp = lake with no governance: nobody can find data, stale vs current unknown, duplicate copies, PII mixed in. Prevent: catalogue at ingest, owners for every dataset, access control, automated quality checks, table formats (Delta Lake / Iceberg) for ACID.

9. Case study: Netflix pipeline (2015–2021)

  • Rate check from the case-study figures:
    1. Events per day ≈ 100,000,000,000.
    2. Seconds per day = 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400.
    3. Average rate = 100,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,157,407 events/s ≈ 1.16 million events/s.
    The stated 1.3 million events/s is a peak-rate figure, which can be above the daily average.
  • All events → Kafka first; then two consumers:
    • Speed: Kafka → Flink (<1 min) → dashboards, alerts, live A/B counters.
    • Batch: Kafka → S3 → Spark + Iceberg (hourly/daily) → ML data, billing.
    • Serving: Cassandra (ms user-state reads), Druid (OLAP).
  • A/B tests (>200 at once): assignment (Cassandra) → exposure event → outcome events → Flink window joins → dashboard refreshed every 5 min.
  • Lessons: Kafka = single source of truth (fixes dual ingestion); 7-day retention enables replay; moving toward Kappa; Schema Registry vital (4,000+ topics); backpressure handled by durable log (Super Bowl 5× spike).
  • Scale: 4,000+ topics, 2,000+ brokers, 150+ Flink jobs, 5,000+ Iceberg tables.

📐 Draw

10. 🧮 Exam-style: bank pipeline (A1)

Needs: (a) 10 M customer records nightly Oracle → Hadoop; (b) fraud decision in 200 ms; (c) dashboard data ≤ 5 min old.

Need Tool Why
(a) Nightly sync Sqoop (incremental import) Bulk, batch, parallel mappers, no streaming needed
(b) Fraud in 200 ms Kafka + Spark Streaming/Flink Real-time stream, low latency, replicated
(c) 5-min dashboard Kafka → stream aggregation → serving store (+ Grafana) Fresh within minutes

Architecture: Lambda fits (batch for accurate nightly reports + speed layer for fraud/dashboard), because regulated banking needs a batch reconciliation. Kappa is wrong when regulation demands separate batch reconciliation.

✅ Week 8 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • Sqoop = bulk RDBMS↔HDFS; Flume = logs→HDFS; Kafka = real-time events; NiFi = visual.
  • Kafka terms: topic, partition, offset (consumer tracks), broker, leader/replica, consumer group (1 partition → 1 consumer).
  • Kafka fast: sequential I/O + zero-copy + batching.
  • Lambda = 3 layers (batch, speed, serving), dual code = weakness.
  • Kappa = log + one stream engine, replay from offset 0.
  • Data lake vs swamp; fix = catalogue + governance + Delta/Iceberg.
  • Netflix: Kafka as single source of truth; Flink (speed) + Spark/Iceberg (batch).
  • Draw: N² mesh vs bus; Lambda; Kappa; Kafka topic; Flume Source-Channel-Sink.

Week 9: Data Visualization — Principles, Techniques & Big Data Tools

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. Why visualise big data?

Anscombe's Quartet (1973): 4 datasets with the same statistics but totally different shapes.

  • Same for all four: mean x = 9.0, mean y = 7.5, variance x = 11.0, correlation r = 0.816, fit line y = 3 + 0.5x.
  • But: I = linear, II = curved, III = has an outlier, IV = vertical cluster.
  • Lesson: always plot the data before trusting statistics.

Big data makes this worse: overlapping groups with opposite trends cancel out; log-scale data makes the mean meaningless; streaming hides sudden changes inside daily averages. Bangladesh example: DGHS yearly average looks flat, but a line chart shows cholera spike Jun–Aug and dengue peak in October.

2. Tufte's principles (1983)

1) Data-ink ratio — maximise it.

Formula: Data-ink ratio = ink that shows data ÷ total ink in the chart

  • Chartjunk (ink that shows no data): heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, gradient fills, borders, redundant legends, "ducks" (decorations that represent themselves), vibrating patterns.
  • Rule: if erasing an element loses no information → erase it.
  • Note: data-ink ratio is about what the ink encodes, not using less ink (MCQ trap).

Before / after (answer for D1):

  • Before: 3-D bars, heavy gridlines, gradient fill, thick border, big title in capitals, redundant legend for one series.
  • After: flat bars, y-axis from 0, no gridlines (or one light line), direct labels, small clean title.

2) Small multiples — same chart repeated for different subsets (district × year) with the same scale → easy comparison. 3) Sparklines — word-sized trend lines inside text/table cells.

Lie Factor (from the Part 2 reading)

Formula: Lie Factor = (relative effect shown by the graphic) ÷ (relative effect in the data)

  • Lie Factor = 1: graphic represents the size of the change proportionally.
  • Greater than 1: graphic exaggerates the change.
  • Less than 1: graphic understates the change.

Illustrative worked example. The numbers below are chosen to demonstrate the formula; they are not presented as a verbatim numerical example from the lecture slide.

  1. Calculate the real change: data increases from 100 to 110.(110 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100% = 10%
  2. See how a misleading axis changes the bar heights: if the y-axis starts at 90, the bar heights are 100 − 90 = 10 and 110 − 90 = 20.
  3. Calculate the change the chart appears to show:(20 − 10) ÷ 10 × 100% = 100%
  4. Calculate the Lie Factor:100% ÷ 10% = 10
  5. Interpretation: the chart makes the 10% real increase look like a 100% increase, exaggerating it by a factor of 10.
  6. Correct the chart: use a zero baseline for a bar chart. Heights 100 and 110 then represent a 10% difference, so the Lie Factor is about 1.

📐 Draw: before vs after

Left: boxed 3-D bars, grid, legend. Right: plain flat bars, axis labels only.

📐 Draw: small multiples & sparkline

3. Shneiderman (1996): "The Eyes Have It"

Mantra: "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand." Step 1 see the whole picture → Step 2 narrow to what matters → Step 3 get the raw record. (Tableau drill-down, Grafana time zoom, Google Maps all follow it.)

7 data types and best charts:

Data type Example Charts
1-D linear Time series, ranked list Bar, histogram
2-D (map) Geographic Choropleth, bubble map
3-D MRI/CT 3-D scatter, volume render
Temporal Timelines Line, area, calendar heatmap
Multi-dimensional Census data Scatter matrix, parallel coords, heatmap
Tree File system, org chart Treemap, sunburst, dendrogram
Network Social graph Force-directed, chord

7 tasks: Overview, Zoom, Filter, Details-on-demand, Relate, History, Extract. (The Part 1 slide lists 5: overview, zoom, filter, details-on-demand, relate.) Treemap (Shneiderman 1991): nested rectangles; area ∝ size, colour ∝ second variable; shows 100,000+ nodes. Dynamic queries: sliders update the picture in <100 ms.

4. Choosing the right chart

Question Use Avoid
Change over time Line, area, calendar heatmap Pie
Which category biggest Horizontal bar (>5 cats), grouped bar 3-D pie
Geographic spread Choropleth (rates), bubble map (counts) Plain bar
Connections Force-directed graph, chord Table
Distribution Histogram, box plot, violin Line
Correlation Scatterplot, scatter matrix Bar
>3 variables Parallel coords, t-SNE/UMAP, clustered heatmap 3-D bar

Pie chart: only for ≤ 4 categories and "part of whole". Humans judge angles worse than bar length.

5. Big data visualization challenges

Challenge 1: Overplotting (millions of points = solid blob)

Three fixes:

  1. Alpha transparency: set each point opacity to α = 0.02. Calculation: 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50, so about 50 fully overlapping points would accumulate to nominal full opacity in the simplified linear model. Dense regions look darker, though blending/compositing details affect exact appearance.
  2. Hexbin: divide the plot into hexagonal cells, count the points in each cell, then colour the cells by count. Average-count estimate:
    1. Points = 10,000,000.
    2. Cells ≈ 10,000.
    3. Average = 10,000,000 ÷ 10,000 ≈ 1,000 points per cell.
    The real count varies by cell; 1,000 is only the average across all cells.
  3. KDE / density contour — estimate smooth density, draw contour lines → shows shape, peaks, tails.

📐 Draw: three panels side by side

Challenge 2: Latency (dashboard must answer in <1 s but table has 100 B rows)

  1. Pre-aggregation / data cube: pre-compute aggregates across dimensions such as date × district × product × channel. Calculation:
    1. Raw fact table: about 100,000,000,000 rows.
    2. Pre-aggregated result queried: about 1,000,000 rows.
    3. Rows-to-scan ratio: 100,000,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 100,000×.
    Approximate reduction in rows scanned: 100,000×. Trade-off: a nightly cube can be up to 24 hours stale and requires storage.
  2. Approximate Query Processing (AQP) — sample-based estimate in ms (Datasketches, BlinkDB). Trades accuracy for speed — OK for dashboards, not for financial reconciliation.

📐 Draw

Challenge 3: Streaming visualization

Pipeline: Event producers → Kafka → Spark Structured Streaming/Flink (e.g., 1-min tumbling window) → Time-series DB (InfluxDB/Prometheus/Elasticsearch) → Grafana/Kibana (refresh ~5 s).

  • Grafana polls the DB every few seconds; for sub-second use WebSocket push (D3.js).

📐 Draw: streaming viz pipeline

6. Tools

Tool Best for Real-time?
Tableau Business dashboards, drag-drop BI Limited
Power BI Microsoft world, executive reports Limited
D3.js Custom interactive web charts (binds data to DOM/SVG) Yes (WebSocket)
Grafana Real-time ops monitoring (InfluxDB, Prometheus) Yes (5 s)
Apache Superset Open-source BI on data lakes (Presto/Hive/Spark SQL), billions of rows Limited
Kibana Log analytics (Elasticsearch only) Yes

Heuristic: business users → Tableau/Power BI; custom web → D3; ops monitoring → Grafana; open BI on Hadoop/Spark lake → Superset. D3 does not produce static PNG/PDF as its main output (T/F False).

7. Part 2 — Tufte & Shneiderman context + NYT case

  • Tufte self-published (every publisher rejected it; >20,000 citations). Central claim: graphical excellence = most ideas, shortest time, least ink, smallest space. He studied ~4,000 charts.
  • Shneiderman (Univ. of Maryland) invented the treemap.
  • NYT Graphics Desk (≈50 people, 6 M readers/day): D3.js (created by Mike Bostock at NYT).
  • COVID tracker (2020–22): Python scrapers → pandas → GitHub CSV → D3 charts, auto-update hourly; loaded 800 M times in 2020.
    • Tufte applied: no gridlines, small multiples (50-state grid).
    • Shneiderman applied: national overview → state dropdown/date slider (zoom/filter) → hover tooltip (details).
    • 7-day rolling average removes day-of-week reporting noise.
  • Lessons: data quality is the hidden half of visualisation; accessibility (colour-blind tests, data table for screen readers); small multiples beat animation; rolling average = editorial choice; open data on GitHub spawned 1,000+ dashboards.

8. 🧮 Exam-style: DGHS dashboard (A1)

Need Chart Shneiderman type Big-data challenge Tool
(a) COVID cases by district, 24 months Choropleth map + small-multiple line charts per district 2-D map + temporal Latency (pre-aggregate by district/month) Superset/Tableau
(b) Hospitalisation rate every 5 min Line chart (live) Temporal Streaming Grafana (Kafka → Spark → InfluxDB)
(c) Age/gender breakdown Grouped/stacked bar or histogram 1-D None (small after aggregation) Tableau/Power BI

Tufte chartjunk to remove: e.g., 3-D effect / gridlines / gradient fill.

✅ Week 9 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • Data-ink ratio = data ink ÷ total ink (not "use less ink"). Remove chartjunk.
  • Lie Factor = effect shown ÷ effect in data (1 = honest).
  • Mantra: overview → zoom & filter → details on demand.
  • 7 data types; 7 tasks. Treemap = area ∝ size.
  • Pie ≤ 4 categories only. Histogram for distribution. Choropleth for geographic.
  • Overplotting fixes: alpha, hexbin, KDE contour.
  • Latency fix: data cube / pre-aggregation (trade-off = staleness); AQP = sampling.
  • Streaming: Kafka → Spark/Flink → TSDB → Grafana.
  • Anscombe: same stats, different pictures.
  • Tools: Grafana = real-time; Superset = open BI on lake; D3 = custom web.

Week 10: Big Data in Real Applications — Social Media, Time Series & Health Data

Official slides · Part 1 · Official slides · Part 2

1. Three domains (shared stack: HDFS/S3, Kafka, Spark, Hive, Grafana/Superset)

Domain Data nature Key methods Tools
Social media Graph, temporal, text, multimedia Community detection, sentiment, influence, trends GraphX, NetworkX, Neo4j
Time series Ordered, seasonal, noisy ARIMA, Prophet, LSTM, anomaly detection Prophet, Spark MLlib, statsmodels
Healthcare EHR, genomics, wearables, imaging, privacy-critical Clinical prediction, privacy methods FHIR, TensorFlow, Spark MLlib

2. Domain A: Social media analytics

4 data dimensions: (1) graph (who follows whom — the graph is the main object), (2) temporal (timestamps, cascades), (3) text/NLP (short, noisy, emojis, code-switching like Bangla-English), (4) multimedia (images, video → computer vision). Bangladesh: Facebook dominant (50 M+ users); crisis info spreads on Facebook pages during floods/cyclones; Bangla misinformation analysis is active research.

Community detection — Louvain algorithm

Community = nodes more densely connected inside than outside. Modularity = fraction of edges inside communities minus the fraction expected by chance. Steps:

  1. Start: every node is its own community.
  2. Move each node to the neighbour community that increases modularity most.
  3. Merge communities into super-nodes.
  4. Repeat until modularity gain is zero. Complexity O(n log n) → works on billion-node graphs (Spark GraphX).

📐 Draw

Influence maximisation

Pick k seed nodes to spread information to the most users. The optimisation problem is NP-hard (Kempe et al., KDD 2003), but a greedy method guarantees at least a fraction (1 − 1/e) of the optimum.
Approximation calculation:

  1. e ≈ 2.718.
  2. 1 ÷ e ≈ 1 ÷ 2.718 ≈ 0.368.
  3. 1 − 0.368 = 0.632.
Result: about 63.2% of the optimal value.

Sentiment — VADER

Lexicon + rule based, made for social media. Handles CAPS, punctuation (!!!), degree words (very), negation (not good), emojis. Output: compound score in [−1, +1]: > 0.05 positive; < −0.05 negative; else neutral. Spark pipeline: UDF on each tweet → aggregate by time window/topic → Grafana.

Trend detection

Look for a sudden spike vs the phrase's own baseline (10/hour → 10,000/hour), regardless of absolute volume (Twitter uses LSH on character n-grams). Ethical risks: sentiment used to suppress dissent or microtarget vulnerable users; need transparency and purpose limitation.

3. Domain B: Time series

What makes it special: order matters (shuffling destroys it) · autocorrelation · seasonality · trend · non-stationarity (fix by differencing).

ARIMA(p, d, q)

  • AR(p) — value depends on past p values.
  • I(d) — difference the series d times to make it stationary.
  • MA(q) — value depends on past q forecast errors.
  • Best for short, stationary, non-seasonal, small data. Limits: needs stationarity, weak with multiple seasonalities, expert tuning → can't hand-fit 10,000 series.

LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)

The lecture lists LSTM as another forecasting option but does not explain it in detail in the available slide outline. As brief supporting background, an LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network designed for ordered data. It uses a memory cell and gates to decide which past information to keep or forget. It can learn complex patterns from long time series, but it usually needs more data, training time, and computing power than simpler models. It is also harder to explain than Prophet. For an exam comparison, remember: ARIMA is a classical statistical model, Prophet is designed for interpretable trend/seasonality/holiday components, and LSTM is a neural-network option for more complex sequential patterns.

Prophet (Taylor & Letham, 2018)

Formula: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t)

  • g(t) trend — piecewise linear or logistic, with automatic changepoints.
  • s(t) seasonality — Fourier series (annual P = 365.25, weekly P = 7), multiple seasonalities.
  • h(t) holidays/events — user-given list (Eid, elections, cricket World Cup).
  • ε(t) — noise.

Piecewise trend: g(t) = (k + a(t)ᵀδ)·t + (m + a(t)ᵀγ) — k = base growth rate, δ = slope changes at changepoints, m = offset. Sparse prior on δ (most ≈ 0) prevents overfitting. Fourier seasonality: s(t) = Σₙ₌₁ᴺ [ aₙ cos(2πnt/P) + bₙ sin(2πnt/P) ] — larger N = wigglier seasonality. Why used: analysts (not statisticians) can tune it, interpretable, handles missing data/outliers, each series fitted independently → embarrassingly parallel. Hyperparameter for trend flexibility: changepoint_prior_scale (e.g., 0.05 → 0.5 = more flexible).

📐 Draw: Prophet decomposition

Anomaly detection

  1. STL decomposition (trend + seasonal + residual): flag residual where |residual| > k × IQR.
  2. Isolation Forest: random trees isolate points; anomalies need fewer splits → shorter path length. No distribution assumption; scales in Spark. bKash: agent jumps from 10 to 10,000 transactions/hour → flagged (possible money laundering).

🧮 Spark batch forecasting (5,000 SKUs)

Week 10 lecture case: forecast 90-day demand for 5,000 store-product (SKU) time series. A sequential run takes 8+ hours; the slide reports about 12 minutes on a 20-executor Spark cluster.

Workflow steps

  1. Load the time series into one Spark DataFrame (one row per day per SKU).
  2. Group by sku_id so each group contains one independent time series.
  3. Use applyInPandas(prophet_fit_and_forecast) to fit a model for each SKU.
  4. Spark distributes the groups across the cluster, allowing many models to run in parallel.
  5. Write forecasts to Hive/S3 in Parquet format for dashboards and downstream use.

Speedup calculation

  1. Convert 8 hours to minutes: 8 × 60 = 480 minutes.
  2. Compare sequential and parallel runtime: 480 ÷ 12 = 40× speedup.

This ratio uses the lecture's approximate runtime values (8 hours and 12 minutes), so the result is an approximate speedup.

4. Domain C: Healthcare big data

Four healthcare data types: (1) EHR (ICD-10 codes, labs, notes; HL7 FHIR); (2) genomics (one genome ≈ 200 GB); (3) wearables/IoT (per-second streams → Kafka); and (4) DICOM medical imaging (CT/MRI 200 MB–2 GB each; unstructured binary data, usually analysed with imaging AI rather than ordinary SQL).

Genomics storage estimate (decimal units)

  1. Approximate size per genome = 200 GB.
  2. Number of patients = 10,000.
  3. Total = 10,000 × 200 GB = 2,000,000 GB.
  4. Convert units: 2,000,000 GB = 2,000 TB ≈ 2 PB (using 1,000 GB = 1 TB and 1,000 TB = 1 PB).

This is a storage-size estimate based on the slide's approximate genome size, before replicas, intermediate files, or analysis outputs.

📐 Draw: health data lake

Clinical prediction (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016): ICU mortality (random forest, AUROC > 0.90), 30-day readmission (gradient boosting, −20% readmissions), sepsis early warning (streaming, ~6 h earlier). Needs ~1 M+ records.

Privacy rules:

Law Key point
HIPAA (USA) Healthcare data; de-identify 18 PHI identifiers; consent
GDPR (EU) Data minimisation, purpose limitation, right to erasure
PDPA Bangladesh Under development, GDPR-like; NID-linked records need explicit consent

Techniques: Safe harbour (remove 18 identifiers) · Expert determination · Differential privacy (add calibrated noise) · Federated learning (train at each hospital, raw data never moves).

AlphaFold (DeepMind, 2020): predicts a protein's 3D structure from its amino-acid sequence. Trained on 170,000 PDB structures; uses MSAs from ~250 M UniProt sequences (Evoformer); 2022 released 200 M predicted structures. Part of the work won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (as noted on the slides).

5. Part 2: Kwak et al. (2010) — "Is Twitter a social network or a news media?"

Data: 41.7 M users, 1.47 B following edges, 106 M tweets, crawled June 2009 (BFS, rate-limited, stored on HDFS, analysed with MapReduce).

Finding Number
Reciprocity (mutual follow) only 22.1% → 77.9% one-way
Follower distribution power law, α ≈ 2.276
Avg shortest path 4.12 hops (small world)
Trending topics that are headline news 85% (15% social memes)
Median trend lifetime 17.5 hours
Breaking news peak within 15 min

Conclusion: Twitter works like a real-time news wire, not a typical social network. → enabled social-media epidemiology (flu estimates ~2 weeks ahead) and misinformation cascade studies.

📐 Draw: directed graph + log-log plot

Social-network reach estimate — assume an average out-degree of 45 (each node reaches 45 new nodes on average). The calculation is an upper-bound branching estimate.

  1. Hop 1: 45 users.
  2. Hop 2: 45 × 45 = 45² = 2,025 possible users.
  3. Hop 3: 45 × 45 × 45 = 45³ = 91,125 possible users.
  4. Total through three hops: 45 + 2,025 + 91,125 = 93,195 possible user-visits (upper bound).

The true number of unique people is usually lower because audiences overlap, accounts may be inactive, and real network degrees are highly uneven.

6. Case study: CDC flu surveillance & Google Flu Trends

  • ILINet: >3,000 sentinel doctors report weekly flu-like illness → 1–2 week lag.
  • BioSense: real-time data from 3,500+ emergency departments (syndromes auto-extracted).
  • Syndromic surveillance = early signals from non-traditional data: tweets (7–10 days before ER visits), pharmacy sales (3–5 days), ER complaints (NLP), search trends.

📐 Draw: pipeline

Google Flu Trends (2008–2015):

  • Used 45 search queries; in-sample r² = 0.97.
  • Failed: over-predicted flu by 2× in 2012–13. Reasons (Lazer et al., Science 2014): big-data hubris (treating big data as a substitute for traditional data), search behaviour/Google's own algorithm changes (not transparent), proxy signals measure anxiety not illness.
  • Lesson: supplement, not replace clinical surveillance. High in-sample r² ≠ good out-of-sample.
  • Better: Prophet nowcasting on BioSense ED visits + Twitter as an extra covariate + ensembles (CDC FluSight).

7. 🧮 Exam-style designs (outline answers)

A1 – Bangladesh flu early warning: (a) Ingest tweets/posts via API → Kafka; pharmacy sales nightly via Sqoop (or Kafka if streaming). (b) Features: NLP flu keywords, VADER sentiment, location, volume spikes; pharmacy: paracetamol/ibuprofen sales spike vs baseline. (c) Model: Prophet (seasonality + holidays) with signals as covariates; validate against DGHS/CDC-style surveillance data (lead time, error). (d) Ethics: privacy, bias, false alarms → anonymise, aggregate, treat as an early signal only. A2 – Supermarket 90-day forecasts: POS → Kafka → HDFS/S3 as Parquet partitioned by date/store; Prophet (multiple seasonality + holidays like Eid; interpretable) rather than ARIMA (hand-tuning) or LSTM (needs more data); parallelise with Spark groupBy(sku).applyInPandas (5,000 models in parallel).

✅ Week 10 — Exam Tips / Important Points

  • Prophet: y = g + s + h + ε (trend, seasonality, holidays, noise); changepoints; Fourier seasonality; scales via Spark.
  • ARIMA(p,d,q) = AR + differencing + MA; stationary, small data.
  • Louvain = modularity-based community detection; influence maximisation NP-hard, greedy (1−1/e).
  • VADER compound in [−1, +1]; thresholds ±0.05.
  • Isolation Forest: short path = anomaly.
  • Kwak: 41.7 M users, 22.1% reciprocity, α ≈ 2.276, 4.12 hops, 85% news.
  • Healthcare: 4 data types; HIPAA 18 identifiers; differential privacy; federated learning.
  • GFT = big data hubris; syndromic surveillance supplements, never replaces.
  • AlphaFold = protein structure from sequence.
  • Time series are order-sensitive (shuffling changes results → True); social graphs are sparse (True).

Overall Summary (Week 5 – Week 10)

Most important things to revise:

  1. YARN (RM / NM / AM, containers, schedulers) — and Parquet vs ORC vs Avro, columnar I/O saving, gzip not splittable (W5).
  2. Spark: RDD (5 properties, lineage), lazy evaluation, transformations vs actions, narrow vs wide, why Spark beats MapReduce on iterations (200× I/O) (W6).
  3. Hive: architecture, Metastore, schema-on-read, partitioning vs bucketing, Presto (W7).
  4. Kafka (topic, partition, offset, consumer group), Sqoop/Flume/Kafka, Lambda vs Kappa, data lake vs swamp (W8).
  5. Visualisation: data-ink ratio, lie factor, Shneiderman's mantra, overplotting/latency/streaming fixes, tool choice (W9).
  6. Applications: Louvain, VADER, Prophet formula, ARIMA, healthcare privacy, Google Flu Trends hubris (W10).

Common diagrams to practise: YARN flow · Parquet layout · Spark architecture & lineage · narrow/wide · Hive architecture · partition tree · Lambda · Kappa · Kafka topic · Prophet decomposition.

Common calculation types: I/O saved by columnar (W5) · YARN capacity planning (W5) · K-means MR vs Spark I/O & time (W6) · bucket sizing (W7) · Kafka throughput ratios (W8) · lie factor (W9) · 3-hop reach and Spark speedups (W10).
